strengths: Meaningful domain extension: Expands surgical triplet detection beyond laparoscopic cholecystectomy (e.g., CholecT50) to robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), capturing substantially higher intraoperative complexity, multi-tool concurrency, and anatomical diversity.

Rigorous, clinically grounded annotation protocol: Employs explicit and standardized temporal boundaries for continuous vs. momentary actions, guided by experienced urologists, which resolves significant ambiguities present in earlier benchmarks.
Dense spatial supervision: Provides high-precision instrument bounding boxes across 60,529 frames and 165,567 triplet instances, closing the gap left by weakly supervised surgical triplet datasets.

Solid baseline benchmarking: Evaluates weakly supervised methods against an extensive suite of modern fully supervised object detectors (Deformable DETR, RT-DETR, YOLOv5 through YOLOv12), and introduces a reasonable baseline (YOLO-Triplet) that provides clear performance benchmarks.
weaknesses: Absence of temporal video models in benchmarking: Despite highlighting the importance of temporal action boundaries and surgical workflow dynamics, all evaluated competitive models are static frame-level 2D object detectors. Benchmarks using spatio-temporal action detectors or video transformers are missing from the main results.

Omission of tracking baseline results in the main text: While Section 6 is dedicated to tracking annotations and introduces the 'Triplet Perspective' for tracking, no tracking metrics (e.g., HOTA, MOTA, IDF1) or tracking baseline experiments are reported in the main manuscript.

Limited patient/video volume: The dataset comprises 21 surgical procedures in total, with only 9 newly collected videos and 12 re-annotated from ESAD and PSI-AVA. With a 14/2/5 train/val/test split, video-level diversity is relatively modest.

Target anatomical structures lack spatial bounding boxes: Grounding is restricted to instrument bounding boxes paired with action and target semantic labels, rather than full relation detection where both instrument and anatomical target are spatially localized.

strengths: Addresses significant limitations of prior surgical triplet benchmarks (such as CholecT50) by providing dense instrument bounding box annotations, standardized temporal action boundaries, and multi-institutional data sources across 60,529 frames and 165,567 triplet instances.

Rigorous, clinically grounded annotation protocol involving over 50 contributors including practicing urologists and medically trained annotators, with explicit definitions distinguishing continuous from momentary actions.
Expands surgical action triplet analysis beyond laparoscopic cholecystectomy to robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), capturing higher multi-tool concurrency and anatomical complexity.

Solid empirical benchmarking comparing weakly supervised triplet baselines with modern object detection frameworks (YOLOv5 through YOLOv12, RT-DETR, Deformable DETR) and a dedicated YOLO-Triplet baseline.
weaknesses: While frame and instance counts are dense, the dataset comprises only 21 surgical procedures (14 train, 2 val, 5 test), which limits inter-patient and inter-surgeon diversity across test splits.

Section 6 introduces tracking perspectives and track ID annotations, but empirical tracking baselines, evaluation protocols (e.g., MOTA, HOTA), and quantitative results are entirely absent from the main manuscript and relegated to the supplement.

The methodological contribution (YOLO-Triplet) yields only marginal improvement in overall triplet detection (36.02% vs 35.05% for YOLOv10) and actually degrades verb and target recognition accuracy compared to standard YOLO detectors, indicating limited effectiveness of the relation modeling head.

Spatial localization is restricted to instrument bounding boxes rather than segmenting or bounding the interacting anatomical target tissues, meaning tissue interaction is localized purely via tool location rather than paired spatial grounding.

strengths: High-impact dataset contribution: The paper addresses a major bottleneck in surgical video understanding by moving beyond laparoscopic cholecystectomy (e.g., CholecT50) to robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), which features higher tool concurrency, intricate anatomical structures, and greater procedural complexity.

Rigor in annotation and clinical grounding: The dataset features dense frame-level bounding boxes for instruments and clearly defined, clinically validated temporal action boundaries distinguishing between continuous and momentary interactions, addressing known ambiguities in existing surgical triplet benchmarks.

Multi-institutional diversity: Incorporating videos from three distinct sources (in-house, PSI-AVA, and ESAD) significantly improves dataset variability and presents a more realistic testbed for model generalizability.

Extensive experimental benchmarking: The authors evaluate multiple paradigms, including weakly supervised baselines, modern transformer-based detectors (Deformable DETR, RT-DETR), and recent YOLO variants (v5 through v12), establishing solid baseline performance metrics for the community.
weaknesses: Modest procedure-level diversity: While the frame and instance counts are large (60,529 frames and 165,567 instances), the dataset comprises only 21 full surgical procedures, with the test set consisting of just 5 videos. A leave-one-center-out or k-fold cross-validation setup would better substantiate cross-domain generalization claims.

Lack of tracking evaluation in the main text: Section 6 motivates and details tracking annotations (Intraoperative and Triplet perspectives), but provides no quantitative benchmark results or baseline comparisons for tracking tasks in the main paper.

Limited methodological innovation: The proposed YOLO-Triplet is a straightforward combination of off-the-shelf detection backbones with a basic cross-attention classification head, yielding marginal gains in triplet mAP (36.02% vs 35.05% for YOLOv10) while incurring a significant frame rate drop.

Missing quantitative inter-annotator reliability: Given that over 50 annotators and multiple iterative correction stages were involved, reporting standard inter-rater agreement statistics (such as Cohen's/Fleiss' Kappa for triplets and bounding box IoU overlap between reviewers) would demonstrate label reliability more rigorously.

strengths: Substantial dataset contribution: ProstaTD addresses a major bottleneck in surgical video understanding by transitioning surgical triplet reasoning from frame-level classification or weakly supervised localization to fully supervised detection with dense bounding boxes across complete procedures.

Rigorous annotation process and clinical reliability: Involves over 60 contributors (including practicing surgeons), multi-institutional sources (ESAD, PSI-AVA, and in-house PWH), clear temporal boundary definitions for actions, and demonstrates solid inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa = 0.82).

Valuable tooling ecosystem: Releasing two purpose-built open-source annotation software tools (Triplet-labelme and SurgLabel) alongside a standardized evaluation toolkit (ivtdmetrics) provides significant utility to the medical computer vision community.

Comprehensive benchmarking: Thorough 5-fold cross-validation benchmark covering classic and recent detectors (Faster R-CNN, Deformable-DETR, RT-DETR, YOLOv10-v12, TAPIR, MCIT-IG), along with a tailored baseline (TDnet) incorporating instance-level distillation and multi-task auxiliary supervision.
weaknesses: Modest procedure count: While the frame and instance counts are large (71k frames, 196k instances), the dataset encompasses only 21 unique surgical videos across three sources (9 newly collected, 12 re-annotated from existing repositories), which may limit procedural and patient diversity.

Target tissue lacks spatial localization: Similar to prior triplet formulations, bounding boxes are assigned strictly to instruments while anatomical targets and verbs are framed as associated categorical attributes rather than spatially grounded objects or interaction pairs.

Limited novelty in the proposed baseline method: TDnet combines an existing YOLOv12 backbone with standard multi-task auxiliary heads and instance-level self-distillation. While effective as a benchmark baseline, the technical innovation of the method itself is relatively incremental.

Under-exploration of temporal architectures: Given that surgical actions (verbs) are inherently dynamic and continuous over time, the benchmark predominantly evaluates 2D per-frame object detectors. Only TAPIR is evaluated as a temporal method, leaving video-level or spatio-temporal action detection backbones largely uninvestigated.

strengths: High-impact dataset contribution: ProstaTD addresses a major bottleneck in surgical video understanding—the lack of dense, precise bounding box annotations in existing procedure-level benchmarks like CholecT50. Providing 196,490 fully supervised triplet instances across 71,775 frames fills a critical gap in moving surgical triplet analysis from image-level classification to fine-grained spatial detection.

Rigorous clinical curation and quality control: The dataset incorporates multi-institutional sources (ESAD, PSI-AVA, and newly acquired PWH) and standardizes temporal boundaries based on surgical semantics. The annotation quality is substantiated by an inter-rater agreement study yielding an average Cohen's Kappa of 0.82 across five independent surgeons.

Valuable community tooling: In addition to the dataset, the authors contribute open-source annotation software (Triplet-labelme and SurgLabel with span-based batch labeling and heuristic tracking) and a standardized evaluation toolkit ('ivtdmetrics') supporting global/video-wise mAP, COCO-style interpolation, and multi-threshold metrics.

Comprehensive benchmarking and solid baseline: The paper benchmarks a diverse set of modern object detectors (Faster R-CNN, RT-DETR, YOLOv10-12, TAPIR, MCIT-IG) under a rigorous 5-fold cross-validation protocol. The proposed TDnet baseline provides an effective reference by integrating multi-task supervision and instance-level self-distillation to handle severe class imbalance.
weaknesses: Relatively small patient/procedure sample size: Although the frame and instance counts are large due to dense temporal sampling, the total number of surgical procedures is 21. While understandable given the heavy annotation burden of surgical videos, patient-level diversity remains somewhat constrained.

Tool-centric bounding boxes rather than interactive pair grounding: Bounding boxes are localized strictly around instruments (heads/joints) rather than grounding both instrument and anatomical target boxes or masks, which leaves target localization implicit within the instrument context.

Limited algorithmic novelty of the proposed baseline: TDnet is primarily a combination of YOLOv12 with standard multi-task auxiliary heads and response-based self-distillation. While well-suited as a baseline for a dataset paper, the methodological innovation is relatively incremental.

Lack of temporal modeling in the baseline detector: Surgical actions and interactions are inherently spatio-temporal processes. While the authors discuss why frame-by-frame detection was chosen over temporal models like TAPIR, the baseline operates purely on static single frames.

strengths: Addresses a crucial limitation in surgical video analysis by bridging surgical action triplet reasoning from weak frame-level classification to fully supervised, instance-level detection with high-precision bounding boxes.

Substantial data collection and curation effort across 21 surgical procedures from three distinct sources (71,775 frames, 196,490 triplet instances), supported by clear medical definitions of temporal action boundaries and verified by an inter-rater agreement study (mean Cohen's Kappa = 0.82).

Valuable open-source infrastructure contributions, including two purpose-built annotation tools (Triplet-labelme and SurgLabel) and an enhanced, standardized evaluation toolkit (ivtdmetrics) that supports COCO-style mAP and video-wise metrics.

Comprehensive experimental benchmarking covering a broad spectrum of classical and modern detection architectures (Faster R-CNN, ViT-Det, RT-DETR, YOLOv10-12, TAPIR, MCIT-IG) under a rigorous 5-fold cross-validation protocol.

Presents a well-motivated baseline method (TDnet) leveraging instance-level self-distillation and multi-task auxiliary heads to mitigate severe long-tail class imbalance, supported by thorough ablations and per-class analyses.
weaknesses: The total number of procedures remains relatively modest at 21 videos, which may limit the broader clinical diversity and case heterogeneity, even though the total frame and instance counts are large.

The methodological contribution (TDnet) is primarily an adaptation of existing paradigms (YOLOv12 with multi-task auxiliary supervision and soft-target distillation); while suitable as a baseline, its algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental.
The core baseline detectors evaluate on static, single frames without effectively exploiting temporal context across video sequences, leaving dynamic temporal modeling mostly as future tracking work.

Bounding boxes localize only the surgical instruments rather than grounding the anatomical targets or interaction regions explicitly with separate spatial bounds or masks, though this is consistent with existing surgical triplet conventions.
